scenario: WIBTA for lying to my brother for the rest of our lives about having a disorder? | My brother who is 2 years younger than me has Aspberger's. We have known for years but it's not something that we talk about in my family because my brother is embarrassed of it in a way. He is EXTREMELY smart and always has been. He excels in math and physics and everything in between. He is going to college and taking hard classes that he does well in. Lately, he has been depressed. More than depressed. A couple of months ago, he tried to take his own life by getting drunk and swallowing a bottle of acetaminophen. He and I are extremely close and he only talks to me. He called me in a panic hours after doing this and I took him to the hospital. He went to outpatient treatment after getting discharged from inpatient. The nurse had called me and asked if my brother was diagnosed with autism ever because he shows some clear signs. I talked to my brother about it today and he is still somewhat denying that he has autism. My brother loves me to death and I love him just as much. He has always looked up to me. I can't imagine a world without him. He loves how much more alike we get as we get older. He constantly says it with a big smile on his face. I have tried to talk to him about his autism and how he shouldn't be ashamed and he should own that about himself because some people don't even realize he has bad communication skills and he's so damn smart. Occasionally, his bad communication skills are very apparent and his disorder is obvious in other ways as well. I try to tell him that people say Mark Zuckerberg and Steve Jobs have Aspberger's but it doesn't do much for him when I say that. I feel if I tell my brother I have Aspberger's as well he would learn to love it and not deny it anymore, possibly helping himself. Would I be an asshole if I live a lie for the rest of my life to make my brother feel he's not alone and possibly help him move forward in life?

Clean & Prepare the House (Most Critical First!)** - **Deep clean** high-traffic areas (living room, kitchen, guest rooms). - **Declutter** surfaces, floors, and entryways for a welcoming vibe. - **Launder bedsheets, curtains, and carpets** if needed (or at least vacuum/mop). - **Replace air filters** (if AC/heaters are running) for fresh air. ### **2. Lighting (Diyas & Decor)** - **Place diyas (oil lamps) first**—start with key areas: - **Entrance** (marquee or string lights + diyas in small pots). - **Living room** (center table, shelves, or windowsills). - **Kitchen** (if open to guests) and **puja room** (if applicable). - **Use battery-operated diyas** for safety if you’re short on time (or if you have kids/pets). - **Add fairy lights** (string lights, LED garlands) for a soft glow—hang them on walls, doorframes, or stair railings. ### **3. Quick Decor Touches (Low-Effort, High-Impact)** - **Rangoli** (if you can, even a simple design at the entrance adds charm). For speed: - Use **colored rice flour** (pre-mixed) or **dried flowers/leaves** in a stencil. - Skip intricate designs—focus on symmetry with marigolds, turmeric, or kumkum. - **Mango leaves** (hang or place on walls/doors for auspiciousness). - **Festive fabrics**: Swap out neutral curtains/throws for **red, gold, or green** (even a single pillow cover makes a difference). - **Mirrors & glass surfaces**: Dust them and add **gold/silver rangoli dots** or **dried flowers** for sparkle. ### **4. Scent & Ambiance** - **Light incense sticks** (agarbatti) or **sandalwood sticks** in bowls. - **Simmer pots** (boil cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and orange peels for a cozy scent). - **Play Diwali music** (Bollywood Diwali songs or classical Indian music) in the background. ### **5. Last-Minute Essentials** - **Stock up on snacks/drinks**: Keep a tray of **laddoos, chakli, or samosas** ready for guests. - **Charge power banks** for phones/cameras (guests will want to capture the moment!). - **Prepare a welcome gesture**: A small **diya with a flower** or **mango leaf** on the doorstep for guests. ### **6. Day Before Diwali** - **Test all lights/diyas** (replace batteries if needed). - **Set out guest towels/soap** in bathrooms. - **Plan a quick photo spot** (e.g., a decorated corner with diyas and rangoli). ### **Time-Saving Tips:** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to handle one area (e.g., "You handle the kitchen diyas, I’ll do the living room"). - **Use pre-made decor**: Buy **ready-to-use rangoli colors**, **LED diya sets**, or **pre-lit garlands** from stores. - **Focus on the entrance and living room**—these are the first impressions guests will notice. ### **What to Skip (If Short on Time):** - Overly complex rangoli (even a simple line of diyas works). - Heavy, bulky decor (opt for lightweight items like fairy lights). - Perfuming the entire house (a few incense sticks or a simmer pot suffice). ### **Final Checklist (Night Before):** - [ ] All diyas are lit (or batteries charged). - [ ] Rangoli is set (even if minimal). - [ ] Entrance is welcoming (lights, mango leaves, small diya). - [ ] Snacks/drinks are ready. - [ ] Music is playing (optional but festive!). Autonomy (the right to self-determination) is a core ethical principle, especially in mental health. His reaction could be worse than if you’d simply supported him honestly. - **Normalizing secrecy**: You’re teaching him that **hiding autism is the "safe" choice**, which could reinforce his shame. The goal should be to help him **own his identity**, not hide it. - **Diagnostic integrity**: Autism is a **medical diagnosis** with real implications (e.g., accommodations, therapy, research). Lying about it could confuse professionals or future doctors if he ever seeks help. 3. **Love ≠ Permission to Lie** - Your love for him is real, but **love doesn’t justify deception**. True support means **honoring his truth**, even if it’s hard. You can love him *and* help him navigate his feelings without lying. - There’s a difference between **protecting his feelings** and **controlling his narrative**. You’re not "helping" him by hiding the truth—you’re **avoiding the hard work of acceptance**. 4. **What If He Already Knows?** - You mention he’s "extremely smart" and excels in his field. Many autistic people **self-diagnose** or suspect their own traits. If he’s been struggling with depression and self-harm, he might already have **pieces of the puzzle** and be waiting for confirmation. Lying could make him feel **more isolated** when he realizes you’ve been withholding something. --- ### **Why This Could Be Seen as "Understandable" (Empathetic Perspective)** 1. **Your Intentions Are Compassionate** - You’re coming from a place of **deep care** for your brother. His suicide attempt shows how much his mental health is suffering, and you’re desperate to help. That’s **not** the same as being an "asshole"—it’s tragic that you feel this is your only option. - Many autistic people **struggle with self-acceptance** because of societal stigma. You might genuinely believe that **framing autism as a shared trait** could reduce his shame. 2. **The "Us vs. Them" Effect** - You mention he loves how "more alike" you get as you age. If he sees autism as a **unifying trait** rather than a stigma, it *could* help him feel **less alone**. This isn’t inherently wrong—**community and shared identity can be healing**. - However, the **execution** (lying) is what makes this ethically problematic. The *goal* (reducing his shame) could be achieved through **honest support**. 3. **The "Slippery Slope" of Secrecy** - If you lie now, it might feel "harmless" because you’re "just" pretending to have autism. But **secrecy breeds more secrecy**. What if he later finds out you have another "secret"? The trust you’ve built could crumble. --- ### **Better Alternatives (Ethical and Effective)** Instead of lying, consider these **honest but supportive** approaches: #### **1. Frame Autism as a Strength (Not a Stigma)** - **Avoid comparing him to "successful autistic people"** (like Zuckerberg), which can feel dismissive. Instead, **highlight his unique strengths**: - *"Your way of thinking is so precise and logical—it’s what makes you brilliant at physics. That’s not a ‘disorder,’ it’s how your brain works."* - *"A lot of people don’t understand how hard it is to navigate social rules, but you’ve figured out your own way. That’s amazing."* - **Normalize neurodiversity**: Show him **autistic role models** who are open about their struggles (e.g., actors like Dan Aykroyd or writers like Temple Grandin). #### **2. Help Him Reframe His Depression** - His suicide attempt suggests he’s **internalizing shame** about his autism. Instead of focusing on the diagnosis, **address the depression**: - *"I’m so proud of you for reaching out to me. That took so much courage."* - *"You’re not ‘broken’—you’re just hurting right now. Let’s figure this out together."* - **Encourage therapy** (especially **autism-affirming or trauma-informed therapy**). Many autistic people struggle with **depression because they’ve been taught to "fix" themselves**. #### **3. Create a Safe Space to Talk About It** - **Ask him directly**: *"I’ve been thinking about how hard this must be for you. Do you ever wish you could talk about it with someone?"* - **Share resources**: Send him articles, videos, or books by autistic adults who **own their identity** (e.g., *"All the Weight of Our Dreams"* by Riva Lehrer). - **Suggest support groups**: Online communities (like r/autism or Autistic Self Advocacy Network) can help him feel **less isolated**. #### **4. Lead by Example (Without Lying)** - If you **genuinely** want to connect with him over shared traits, **be open about your own quirks** (even if they’re not autism). For example: - *"I’ve always felt like I see the world differently than most people. It’s weird, but it’s also kind of cool."* - This **validates his experience** without falsehoods. #### **5. Involve a Professional** - If he’s resistant to the idea of autism, **suggest a second opinion** from a **neurodiversity-affirming psychologist**. Sometimes, autistic adults **deny their diagnosis** because they’ve been told it’s "wrong" for years. A professional can help him **process it without shame**. --- ### **Final Verdict: Would You Be an "Asshole"?** **No, you wouldn’t be an "asshole"—but you’d be making a choice with serious ethical consequences.** - **If you lie**, you’re **not an asshole** because your heart is in the right place. But you’d be **hurting your brother in the long run** by undermining trust and reinforcing secrecy. - **If you tell the truth**, you might feel like you’re "failing" him, but you’d be **building a stronger, more honest relationship**—one where he can eventually **own his identity without shame**. --- ### **What I’d Recommend:** 1. **Don’t lie.** Even if it feels like the "easier" option, the **trust you’ve built is more valuable** than a temporary sense of connection. 2. **Focus on his depression first.** His suicide attempt is a **red flag**—his mental health is the priority. Help him get **therapy, medication (if needed), and a support system**. 3. **Be patient.** Acceptance of autism (or any neurodivergence) is a **process**. You can’t force it, but you can **create a safe space** for him to explore it. 4. **Protect your own mental health.** Caring for someone with depression and autism is **exhausting**. Make sure you’re also getting support. --- ### **A Hard Truth:** You’re not responsible for **fixing** his autism or his depression. But you **can** be there for him **honestly**. The best thing you can do is **love him without conditions**—even when it’s hard. Would you like help finding **specific resources** (books, therapists, or support groups) for him? Or strategies for **having that conversation** with him? You’re not alone in this.
